<!-- Not frozen: the next-delivery include reads _variables.yml at render time,
and under freeze Quarto would key the cache on the source of this page alone,
so flipping delivery.active would have no effect. The page therefore runs R in
CI, which installs knitr, rmarkdown and yaml for the render and readr and
datawizard for the chunk below (.github/workflows/publish.yml); a package that
the chunk starts to use has to be added there too.

The page uses the custom layout of the opening pages of the AR4DS sites: every
section is a fenced div with a home- class (styled in style/home.css), and the
format cards, the tasks and all the text are ordinary Markdown below. The
claim, the replication and the reproduction come from the facts file of the
case study (D:\ACADEMIC\TEACHING\AR4DS\_planning\housing\housing-facts.md); the
other numbers are read from the committed data files by the chunk below. -->

```{r}
#| label: numbers
#| include: false
# Numbers quoted on the page, read from the committed data files of the case study;
# the ends of the curve carry a true minus sign.
h_curve <- readr::read_csv("data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
h_analysts <- readr::read_csv("data/analysts5.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
h_emails <- nrow(readr::read_csv("data/housing_emails.csv", show_col_types = FALSE))
coded <- readr::read_csv("data/housing_original.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(ProperName)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hispanic_name = startsWith(TreatmentGroup, "Hispanic"))
tab_8ptrz <- xtabs(~ hispanic_name + ProperName, data = coded)

h_spec <- nrow(h_curve)
h_sig <- sum(h_curve$b_pp < 0 & h_curve$p < 0.05)
h_sig_txt <- if (h_sig == h_spec) "every one of them" else paste(h_sig, "of them")
h_for <- sum(h_analysts$task1 == "evidence for the claim")
h_for_txt <- c("None", "One", "Two", "Three", "Four", "Five")[h_for + 1]
h_ends <- sub("^-", "\u2212", formatC(range(h_curve$b_pp), format = "f", digits = 1))
chi_8ptrz <- formatC(h_analysts$statistic_recorded[h_analysts$id == "8PTRZ"], format = "f", digits = 3)
chi_plain <- formatC(unname(chisq.test(tab_8ptrz, correct = FALSE)$statistic), format = "f", digits = 2)
```

# Housing and racial bias {#housing-and-racial-bias .unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.home-lead}
This site teaches reproduction, robustness and replication in R on one published claim, together with the reanalyses that the claim received in a many-analyst study and the replication that tested it with new data. It is part of Applied Replication for Data Skills (AR4DS).
:::

## The case study {#the-case .unnumbered}

::: {.home-intro}
A field experiment published in 2017 sent the same short email to about a thousand public housing authorities in the United States, each signed with one of six names meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic sender. One sentence of its abstract became the claim that the course works on.
:::

> "Hispanic housing applicants were ... less likely to be greeted by name than were ... white counterparts" [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect, abstract]

The background page tells the story in six parts: the original study and its design, SCORE and its robustness study [Multi100\; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness], the five reanalyses, their effect sizes on the scale of the robustness study, the replication with new data, and the data that you will use. The case study teaches proportions and the chi-square test, the linear probability model set against the logit, what conditioning on a reply does to an experiment, randomisation inference and statistical power, on one file of `r format(h_emails, big.mark = ",")` emails, released into the public domain (CC0) and shipped with the workspace.

::: {.home-cta}
[Read the background](background.qmd)
:::

::::

:::: {.home-rs .home-reveal}

::: {.home-r}
### Reproduction {.unnumbered .unlisted}

SCORE never attempted one, although the data and code are public. The four statistics recorded in the robustness study for the analysts reproduce exactly from the public file.
:::

::: {.home-r}
### Robustness {.unnumbered .unlisted}

`r h_for_txt` of the five analysts of the robustness study found evidence for the claim. The `r h_spec` specifications of the curve of the claim put the gap between `r h_ends[1]` and `r h_ends[2]` percentage points, `r h_sig_txt` significant at 5%.
:::

::: {.home-r}
### Replication {.unnumbered .unlisted}

A preregistered experiment on 3,050 housing authorities, with new names, found no significant gap (z = 0.66, p = 0.51).
:::

## The exercise {.unnumbered .home-reveal}

::: {.home-intro .home-reveal}
Every format works through the same five tasks, or a selection of them. The short format takes the first four and sends nothing to the class chart, while the day and independent formats take all five. The decisions that the tasks ask for fall into three groups: the question that the analysis answers; measurement, how the variables are built; and the model, how it is fitted and its uncertainty judged.
:::

:::: {.home-reveal}

<details>
<summary><span class="home-n">Task 1</span>The setup check</summary>

Check that your tools work before the rest of the work depends on them: the check script of the workspace, or in the short format the setup cell of the deck.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="home-n">Task 2</span>The data, the estimand and the graph</summary>

Meet the data of the case study, write the estimand statement behind the claim, and finish the causal graph that goes with it. The graph shows why a comparison of greetings among the replies alone is no longer protected by the random assignment.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="home-n">Task 3</span>The reproduction</summary>

Choose one of the five analysts and reproduce the value recorded in the robustness study for that analyst, from the public file of the original authors (OAs). The four analysts who recorded a statistic reproduce exactly. One of them, 8PTRZ, recorded $\chi^2$ = `r chi_8ptrz` where the plain test gives `r chi_plain`, and finding out why is part of the task.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="home-n">Task 4</span>The menu</summary>

Work through the decisions that lie between the data and a result, try alternatives one change at a time, and send one exploration to the class chart. The [decision map](menu.qmd#map) lays every decision out.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="home-n">Task 5</span>Preregistration</summary>

Declare one specification in a short preregistration, run it, report it, and find where it sits among the `r h_spec` specifications of the [curve of the claim](curve.qmd).

</details>

::::

The exercise page of each format sets out its tasks, with the tool in which each is done, for the [short](tracks/short/exercise.qmd), [day](tracks/day/exercise.qmd) and [independent](tracks/independent/exercise.qmd) formats.

## The course {.unnumbered .home-reveal}

:::: {.home-reveal}

<details>
<summary>What the course teaches</summary>

The main aim of the course is to introduce technical skills for modern empirical data analysis: finding the data and code of a study in an online repository, working with code so that another person (or your future self) can reproduce your steps, fixing your analytical choices in a preregistration before you run the analysis, and writing a live report that combines code and text. The exercise follows the design of the robustness study on a smaller scale, with many analysts testing the same claim, each stating their analytical choices, and results reported in a form that allows them to be compared.

</details>

<details>
<summary>The companion</summary>

The [companion](companion/index.qmd) holds the teaching material of the course on this case study, in three groups: tools, data and sharing, and methods. Every module keeps its own page and stands on its own, so you can read one for the skill that it covers or take it in the place that a format gives it.

</details>

<details>
<summary>SCORE</summary>

The claim comes from the work of SCORE, a programme that put claims from published social and behavioural research through reproduction, robustness checks and replication. The AR4DS site describes [the programme](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/score.html), and its page on [the robustness article](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/robustness-article.html) explains how the results of the analysts were placed on one scale and compared.

</details>

## Getting started {.unnumbered .home-reveal}

::: {.home-intro .home-reveal}
The short format needs only a browser, because every task of the format is done in its deck, which runs R inside the browser. The day and independent formats do the tasks in the workspace, in your IDE, and install R, an IDE and the workspace as part of their preparation.
:::

:::: {.home-steps .home-reveal}

::: {.home-step}
### R and an IDE {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Install R, Quarto and an IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.), following the steps for your operating system; the short format needs none of them. [Install and check](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/setup.html)
:::

::: {.home-step}
### The workspace {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Download the workspace of the case study as a zip file, open it in your IDE and run the check script. The day and independent formats do their tasks in it. [The workspace](tracks/day/before.qmd#the-workspace)
:::

::: {.home-step}
### The deck {.unnumbered .unlisted}

The decks of the short and day formats run R inside the browser. The short format does every task in its deck, and in the day format the deck shows each step with its output. [Choose a format](#formats)
:::

::: {.home-step}
### The browser lab {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Try the exercise in the browser, without installing anything. With the deck, it is also the fallback when a machine fails on the day. [Open the browser lab](lab.qmd)
:::

## Chris Moreh {.unnumbered}

::: {.home-role}
Lecturer in Sociology, Newcastle University
:::

<!-- The biography is quoted from chrismoreh.com (source: D:/GitHub/chrismoreh-source/index.qmd), as CM asked on 2026-10-25, and copied verbatim from the opening page of the site of the Europeanisation case study. -->

A social scientist interested in the political sociology of migration, mobility, ethnicity and nationalism.

Hailing from Transylvania, trained in anthropology and sociology at [Eötvös Loránd University of Budapest](https://tatk.elte.hu/en/) and [Central European University](https://sociology.ceu.edu/), and with a PhD from [Northumbria University](https://www.northumbria.ac.uk/), I currently work as a Lecturer (Assistant Professor) in Sociology at [Newcastle University (UK)](https://www.ncl.ac.uk/gps/staff/profile/chrismoreh.html).

I approach social research as a comparative, interdisciplinary and multimethodological endeavour. My work has combined ethnographic observation, document analysis, survey methods and statistical modelling.

I'm enthusiastic about transparency and reproducibility in the social sciences, and my [pedagogical approach](https://www.ncl.ac.uk/mediav8/library/file-downloads/research-services/open-research/moreh.pdf) seeks to develop skills that facilitate open and credible research practices.

[chrismoreh.com](https://chrismoreh.com)
